newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sues UPS for alleged discrimination.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sues UPS for alleged discrimination.

text.p: The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Thursday sued package delivery giant United Parcel Service of America Inc., alleging it violated the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The national class action lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in northern California, alleges that UPS unlawfully discriminated against employees who had sight in only one eye by refusing to let them drive delivery trucks.
The suit alleges violations occurred at its facilities in Oakland, Richmond and Petaluma, Calif., as well as elsewhere in the United States.

"We have people who have been able to drive, are cleared to drive, but yet UPS assumed that these people cannot do the job. That's a clear violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act," said William Tamayo, an attorney with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Tamayo said the drivers' union had identified 40 people nationwide who could be covered by the lawsuit. He added that this number could be higher because it would include people with impaired vision who may have been discouraged from applying to drive for UPS.
A spokesperson for UPS, the world's largest package distribution company, was not immediately available to comment on the lawsuit.
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is seeking a court order to bar the company from engaging in any employment practice that discriminates on the basis of disability.
It also seeks an order requiring the company to institute programmes to provide equal employment opportunities for qualified people with disabilities.

The suit seeks back pay and compensation for those allegedly hurt by UPS as well as for unspecified punitive damages. Tamayo said the maximum a plaintiff can receive under the Americans with Disabilities Act is back pay plus up to $300,000 each for compensatory and punitive damages.
He said if the courts find UPS at fault, damages could be in the millions of dollars.
The lawsuit names three people who filed charges with the commission alleging UPS violated the Americans with Disabilities Act.

They included Yvonne Harbison, who was employed as a package car driver at UPS's Oakland facility for nearly 14 years when she lost sight in her left eye due to a medical condition, the commission said.

In 1994, after being released to return to work, UPS refused to let Harbison drive some of its smaller delivery trucks even though she was qualified. Instead, she was transferred against her will to non-driving jobs, including a position handling hazardous materials, the commission said.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission alleged UPS was aware not only that Harbison had been licensed by the California Department of Motor Vehicles to drive with vision in one eye, but that her visual impairment could be easily accommodated.
After Harbison filed her complaint with the commission, she was allowed to resume driving for UPS using its smaller delivery vehicles.
UPS employs more than 339,000 people worldwide and provides services in more than 200 countries and territories.
